doc.title: John Pizzarelli, Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 29, 2000 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Duo with Bucky and the seven-string
title: Mike Tapplinger and the seven-string guitar
summary: A camp friend who studied with Barry Galbraith leads to John playing seven-string; later two-seven-string duets with Bucky.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up a first guitar or banjo, self-taught

blocks.x: It was fun. I think, and then I started to play, I met a kid at this day camp I was working at. Because the only other job I ever had was a day camp counselor. And I like working with kids and I had a lot of fun doing it. And I had been there as a camper and I just stayed there and made a little money in the summer. And there was a guy there who studied with Barry Galbraith, who is a great guitar player, played rhythm guitar on every record you would own. He’s on Clifford Brown Strings and he’s on all the Tony Bennett records, and one of my father’s main influences, favorite rhythm guitar players. And he was a great teacher, he had a studio in the Ed Sullivan building. And this kid Mike Tapplinger had studied with him and knew of my dad, and he met me at camp, and he said, “You’re Bucky Pizzarelli’s son, oh gee, we should get together and play.” So I went to his house — actually he came to my house — and my father said, “you should play seven string behind him.” And I said oh, okay. And he showed me a couple of little tricks. And I had already picked it up and he showed me how to play “Watch What Happens” on it. And there was not a lot of difference for me. I said oh okay, I saw what the deal was. And I started to accompany him and I got a little idea, oh okay, I see how this works. And long story short, that turned into when I came back from college I started playing duets with my dad, like I was saying like concerts, so I knew six more songs so I came up earlier in the show.

Sometimes we’d do the whole night together. And then one day we were doing a concert out in Morristown at a library, and he said, “Play the seven today, we’ll both play sevens. This way when I solo you accompany me, and when you solo I’ll accompany you, we’ll have the two sevens going.” Sure. So the hardest thing was playing “Chicken a la Swing” and forgetting about the other string. And it was fun. And from there on in it was two times seven. © Fillius Jazz Archive -4-
